To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
stem cells of various tissues appear to divide very rapidly during early life, and that the self‐replication potential of hematopoiesis‐related stem cells is directly correlated with telomere length.
telomere length of hematopoietict stem cells in newborn baboons declines rapidly during the first 1 year after birth, and that after this period the stem cell turnover is markedly decreased.
the telomeres of baboon hematopoietic progenitor cells shorten rapidly in the first year of postnatal life.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of stem cell function and its relationship to telomeres and telomerase.
the question whether telomeres are the clock that counts the number of cell divisions.
the relationship between telomere length and the number of times a stem cell has divided.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
telomeres in stem cell populations are not stable and that stem cell turnover rates are not constant during a life span, but rather that they change with time.
the stem cell turnover rate is high in the first year of post‐natal life, but then declines dramatically.
telomeres shorten during the first year after a stem cell is formed, and that the rate of shortening is related to the number of times the stem cell has divided.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stem cells divide very fast in the first year of human life, then slow down, and finally stop.
telomere‐shortening in stem cells is a consequence of the stem cell division, but not the cause of the stem cell aging.
stem cell turnover is highest in the first year of human life.
The main takeaway from our work is that
longitudinal data on telomeres are required for accurate estimation of the number of times cells have divided.
telomere‐shortening data can be used to infer stem cell dynamics, and that such dynamics can change over time.
telomeres in stem cells shorten at a rate that is dependent on stem cell turnover.
